title: Primary, Diagnostic, and Guardrail Metrics
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Primary, Diagnostic, and Guardrail Metrics. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A primary metric determines whether the change achieved the intended result. Preselecting it prevents teams from declaring success using whichever of many outcomes happens to look positive.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at metric roles answer different questions?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Diagnostic metrics test the behavioural chain and help explain why the primary moved or did not move. They can include exposure, intermediate action, state transition, segment, performance, and service operations. Diagnostics support interpretation; they should not become a fishing expedition for wins.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Guardrail metrics protect qualities the team is not trying to optimise but refuses to damage. Organisational guardrails may include latency, crashes, support burden, and revenue. Human guardrails may include errors, unwanted contact, accessibility, safety, privacy, trust, cancellation, and unequal outcomes.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Trustworthiness checks determine whether the experiment and data are believable: sample-ratio mismatch, assignment/exposure anomalies, missing events, logging differences, bots, carryover, and interference. They are not product outcomes. A positive primary result is unusable when randomisation or telemetry is broken.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: One metric can play different roles in different experiments. Appointment latency may be primary for a scheduling intervention and a guardrail for a comprehension change.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at design a metric tree?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Begin with the OEC and causal chain. Place the primary metric at the decision level. Under it, map expected drivers and countervailing paths. For each node define direction, unit, population, window, expected timing, and what movement would mean.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Keep the tree selective. More metrics increase the chance of random movement and contradictory stories. Classify exploratory measures explicitly and use appropriate statistical treatment. Define guardrail thresholds from consequence and baseline variability—not after an attractive result appears.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Add segment views where the mechanism or harm may differ, but do not turn dozens of slices into unplanned significance hunting. Pre-specify critical segments, especially groups exposed to unequal risk.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: search redesign?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Primary success might be successful search sessions or downstream task completion. Query reformulation, result click, quick return, and zero-result rate are diagnostics. Latency, crashes, offensive results, accessibility, and overall site success are guardrails. Click-through alone is dangerous: irrelevant but sensational results can raise it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at interpret patterns, not isolated arrows?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: If the primary is neutral and exposure is low, the idea may not have received a fair test. If proximal diagnostics move but the outcome does not, the assumed causal link may be weak. If the primary improves and a guardrail worsens, apply the pre-agreed rule. If only a subgroup changes, ask whether this was predicted, powered, and consequential.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Do not require every diagnostic to move. Their purpose is to discriminate explanations. Preserve null results and unexpected paths; they improve the behavioural model.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Metric soup: many measures have no assigned role or hierarchy. Primary switching: the winner is chosen after results are visible. Guardrail decoration: harms are monitored without thresholds or authority. Diagnostic promotion: a local click becomes proof of value. Trust-check neglect: broken assignment or logging is analysed as product behaviour.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Aggregate safety: subgroup harm disappears inside overall improvement.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Build a metric set that can explain movement
turns.text: What changes when we look at build a metric set that can explain movement?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: He predefines how trade-offs will be interpreted. A primary improvement with a safety or equity guardrail breach does not pass. A flat primary with improved comprehension may indicate the mechanism changed but follow-up is too short—or the causal model is wrong. Metrics support judgment when they are read together, not when a single number is crowned after the result.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Metric architecture distributes decision rights. Name who owns the primary, who can stop on safety or accessibility guardrails, and who investigates data-quality failures. Guardrails require operational response; a dashboard no one watches is not protection. Review the tree as the product and its incentives evolve.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Give every metric a role in the decision system
turns.text: What changes when we look at give every metric a role in the decision system?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Definitions include denominator, eligibility, event source, time window, segmentation, missingness, and owner. The team inspects distributions and cohorts rather than averages alone. When the primary improves but a guardrail worsens, the result is a trade-off to investigate—not success with an inconvenient footnote.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: <! -- Editorial: manual revision; curated product example --

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a checkout. The primary measure is completed, valid orders. Diagnostic measures show where shoppers drop out or retry payment. Guardrails watch accidental subscriptions, refund requests, support contact, and accessibility failures. When conversion rises but refunds rise too, the metric roles stop the team from calling the experiment a straightforward win.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Find an experiment case study reporting one success metric. Build the missing diagnostic and guardrail tree. What rival explanation remains plausible because the case did not report those measures?
